content: HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin) shows your average blood sugar over the past two to three months. It is reported as a percentage. A single blood sample is enough and you do not need to be fasting.
title: Hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) Test

content: For HbA1c, below 5.7% is normal, 5.7% to 6.4% is the pre-diabetes range (higher-than-normal sugar that raises future diabetes risk), and 6.5% or above suggests diabetes. These cut-offs are used in India and internationally.
title: ICMR Guidelines for Management of Type 2 Diabetes

content: Diabetes and pre-diabetes are very common in India, and they often appear at a younger age and lower body weight than in Western populations, so a raised HbA1c should be taken seriously even if you feel well.
title: ICMR-INDIAB national diabetes study

content: To help bring blood sugar down, Indian dietary guidance suggests replacing refined grains like maida and white rice with whole grains and millets, eating more pulses and vegetables, cutting sugary drinks and sweets, and being physically active on most days.
title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians

content: Fasting blood glucose measures your blood sugar after not eating for at least 8 hours. It is a common test to screen for diabetes.
title: Blood Glucose Test

content: For fasting blood glucose, below 100 mg/dL is normal, 100 to 125 mg/dL is pre-diabetes, and 126 mg/dL or higher on more than one test suggests diabetes.
title: Classification and Diagnosis of Diabetes

content: Low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia), often below about 70 mg/dL, can cause shakiness, sweating, and dizziness. It is more of a concern in people taking diabetes medicines and should be discussed with a doctor.
title: Low Blood Sugar

content: LDL cholesterol is often called the 'bad' cholesterol because high levels can build up in blood vessels and raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
title: LDL and HDL Cholesterol

content: For LDL cholesterol, under 100 mg/dL is optimal, 130 to 159 mg/dL is borderline high, and 160 mg/dL or above is high. South Asians, including Indians, tend to develop heart disease earlier, so keeping LDL low is especially important.
title: Cardiovascular risk and lipids

content: To lower LDL cholesterol, Indian dietary guidance suggests reducing fried foods, vanaspati and reused cooking oil, choosing more vegetables, whole grains and pulses, and being regularly active. Your doctor may add medicine if levels are very high.
title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians

content: HDL cholesterol is the 'good' cholesterol that helps remove excess cholesterol from the blood. Higher levels are protective for the heart.
title: LDL and HDL Cholesterol

content: HDL cholesterol below about 40 mg/dL in men and 50 mg/dL in women is considered low and slightly raises heart risk. Regular physical activity and avoiding tobacco can help raise HDL.
title: HDL cholesterol

content: Triglycerides are a type of fat in the blood. High levels, often linked to excess sugar, refined carbohydrates and alcohol, can raise the risk of heart disease.
title: Triglycerides Test

content: For triglycerides, under 150 mg/dL is normal, 150 to 199 mg/dL is borderline high, and 200 mg/dL or above is high. Cutting sugary foods, sweets and alcohol and increasing activity usually helps.
title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians

content: Total cholesterol is the overall amount of cholesterol in your blood. Desirable is under 200 mg/dL, 200 to 239 is borderline high, and 240 or above is high.
title: Total cholesterol

content: Haemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen around the body. Low haemoglobin means anaemia, which can cause tiredness, weakness and breathlessness.
title: Hemoglobin Test

content: Anaemia (low haemoglobin) is usually diagnosed below about 13 g/dL in men and 12 g/dL in non-pregnant women. Anaemia is very common in India, especially among women and girls, and iron deficiency is a frequent cause.
title: Anaemia thresholds and prevalence

content: For iron-deficiency anaemia, Indian dietary guidance suggests iron-rich foods such as green leafy vegetables, pulses, and jaggery, eaten with a source of vitamin C like lemon or amla to help absorption. Your doctor may advise iron supplements.
title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians

content: Ferritin reflects the body's stored iron. Low ferritin (often under about 30 ng/mL) points to iron deficiency, a common cause of anaemia, and is frequently seen in India.
title: Serum ferritin and iron status

content: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium and keep bones strong. A level below about 20 ng/mL is considered deficient. Vitamin D deficiency is very common in India even though there is plenty of sunlight, partly due to indoor lifestyles and skin covering.
title: Vitamin D status in India

content: To improve vitamin D, spend some time in morning sunlight, and include sources such as fortified milk, eggs and fatty fish where possible. Your doctor may prescribe a vitamin D supplement if levels are low.
title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians

content: Vitamin B12 is needed for healthy nerves and red blood cells. A level below about 200 pg/mL is usually considered low, which can cause tiredness, tingling and anaemia.
title: Vitamin B12 Test

content: Vitamin B12 deficiency is common among vegetarians in India because B12 comes mainly from animal foods. Sources include dairy and eggs, and fortified foods; strict vegetarians and vegans often need a B12 supplement, so discuss this with your doctor.
title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians

content: TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) tells how well your thyroid gland is working. The usual normal range is about 0.4 to 4.0 mIU/L, though labs vary.
title: TSH (Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone) Test

content: A high TSH usually means an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism), which can cause tiredness, weight gain and feeling cold. Hypothyroidism is common in India. Treatment, if needed, is guided by your doctor.
title: Hypothyroidism in India

content: A low TSH usually means an overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism), which can cause a fast heartbeat, weight loss and anxiety, and should be evaluated by a doctor.
title: Hyperthyroidism

content: Creatinine is a waste product filtered by the kidneys. A higher-than-normal blood creatinine can suggest the kidneys are not filtering as well as they should.
title: Creatinine Test

content: eGFR estimates how well the kidneys filter blood. An eGFR of 90 or above is generally normal; below 60 for three months or more suggests chronic kidney disease and needs medical follow-up. Normal creatinine ranges differ slightly for men and women.
title: eGFR and kidney function

content: To protect the kidneys, general advice is to stay well hydrated, limit excess salt, keep blood pressure and blood sugar controlled, and avoid unnecessary painkillers. Your doctor will interpret kidney results along with your history.
title: Kidney health and salt

content: Uric acid is a waste product in the blood. High levels (often above about 7 mg/dL in men and 6 mg/dL in women) can cause gout, a painful joint condition, and are linked to diet and alcohol.
title: Uric Acid Test

content: To lower uric acid, general advice is to drink more water, cut down on alcohol and sugary drinks, and reduce very high-purine foods such as organ meats. Your doctor may advise medicines if gout is frequent.
title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians

content: ALT and AST are liver enzymes. Higher-than-normal levels can be a sign of liver inflammation or fatty liver, which is increasingly common in India due to changing diets and weight gain.
title: ALT and AST Blood Tests

content: For a healthier liver, general advice is to limit alcohol, reduce sugary and fried foods, stay active, and reach a healthy weight. Fatty liver often improves with these steps; your doctor may suggest further tests if enzymes stay high.
title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians

content: Bilirubin is a yellow substance made when red blood cells break down. Mildly high bilirubin is often harmless (for example, Gilbert's syndrome), but higher levels can relate to the liver or gallbladder and should be reviewed by a doctor.
title: Bilirubin Blood Test

content: White blood cells (WBC) help fight infection. A high WBC count often points to an infection or inflammation, while a low count can occur with some viral infections or medicines. It is interpreted along with your symptoms.
title: White Blood Count (WBC)

content: Platelets help blood to clot. A low platelet count can occur with infections such as dengue, which is common in India, while a very high count is less common; significant changes should be discussed with a doctor.
title: Platelet Tests

content: Overweight and obesity raise the risk of diabetes, heart disease and fatty liver. For Asian Indians, a BMI of 23 or above is already considered overweight and 25 or above obese, which is lower than the cut-offs used for Western populations.
title: Asian Indian BMI cut-offs

content: General healthy-living advice from Indian dietary guidelines includes eating a variety of whole grains, pulses, vegetables and fruit, using iodised salt in moderation, limiting sugar, salt and ultra-processed foods, staying physically active, and avoiding tobacco.
title: Dietary Guidelines for Indians
